name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q01 - Sequence of events in micturition reflex

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following physiological events occurring during the micturition reflex in the correct chronological sequence:

  1. Stretch receptors on the wall of the urinary bladder send afferent signals to the Central Nervous System (CNS).
  2. Urine progressively accumulates in the urinary bladder, leading to stretching of the bladder wall.
  3. Smooth muscles of the urinary bladder contract while the urethral sphincter relaxes simultaneously.
  4. The CNS processes the afferent input and transmits motor messages to the urinary bladder.
  5. Release and expulsion of urine occurs through the urethra.

Choose the correct option representing the proper sequence:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Micturition is the neural reflex mechanism by which urine temporarily stored in the urinary bladder is expelled under coordinated voluntary and autonomic control.

Step 2: Sensory Activation Sequence
Urine formed continuously by the nephrons enters the urinary bladder via the ureters. As the volume of urine increases, the bladder wall stretches progressively. This physical distension stimulates stretch receptors embedded within the bladder wall, which generate action potentials that travel as afferent sensory signals to the Central Nervous System (CNS).

Step 3: Motor Response and Efferent Action
Upon integrating the sensory input, the CNS generates motor impulses that travel via autonomic efferent pathways to the effector tissues. These signals initiate the contraction of the smooth muscles of the bladder body and cause simultaneous relaxation of the urethral sphincter guarding the bladder neck.

Step 4: Mechanical Expulsion
The resulting rise in intravesical pressure overcomes urethral resistance, culminating in the outflow and release of urine through the urethra.

Step 5: Final Answer
The correct physiological order begins with urine accumulation and stretching of the bladder wall, followed by activation of stretch receptors sending signals to the CNS, then transmission of motor messages from the CNS, subsequent contraction of bladder smooth muscle with simultaneous relaxation of the urethral sphincter, and finally the expulsion of urine through the urethra (II → I → IV → III → V).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q02 - Sequence of renin angiotensin aldosterone activation pathway

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following physiological steps of the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone mechanism in the correct chronological sequence following an acute reduction in body fluid volume:

  1. Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells get activated to secrete the enzyme renin into systemic circulation.
  2. Angiotensin II stimulates the adrenal cortex to synthesize and release aldosterone.
  3. A decrease occurs in glomerular blood flow, glomerular blood pressure, or glomerular filtration rate (GFR).
  4. Aldosterone drives conditional reabsorption of Na\(^+\) and water from distal segments of the nephron.
  5. Renin enzymatically converts plasma angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.
  6. Angiotensin I is further converted into the powerful vasoconstrictor angiotensin II.

Choose the correct sequence from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis operates as an essential neuroendocrine autoregulatory feedback loop to restore arterial blood pressure, renal perfusion, and glomerular filtration rate when hypovolemia or hypotension occurs.

Step 2: Sensory Trigger and Renin Release
A decrease in systemic blood volume or renal perfusion pressure manifests as a reduction in glomerular blood flow, glomerular capillary blood pressure, or GFR. This hemodynamic decline serves as the initial trigger sensed by the juxtaglomerular apparatus, prompting JG cells to release renin into the bloodstream.

Step 3: Enzymatic Cascade and Angiotensin II Production
Circulating renin cleaves hepatic angiotensinogen into decapeptide angiotensin I. Angiotensin I is subsequently converted into octapeptide angiotensin II, which exerts potent systemic vasoconstriction to elevate perfusion pressure.

Step 4: Endocrine Release and Tubular Reabsorption
Angiotensin II acts upon the adrenal cortex, stimulating the secretion of the mineralocorticoid hormone aldosterone. Aldosterone acts directly on the principal cells of the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct to enhance the reabsorption of sodium ions and water into the peritubular capillaries, thereby restoring intravascular volume and returning GFR back to homeostatic levels.

Step 5: Final Answer
The chronological sequence starts with a fall in glomerular flow/pressure/GFR, followed by JG cell activation releasing renin, conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, release of aldosterone from the adrenal cortex, and ends with aldosterone-mediated reabsorption of Na\(^+\) and water from the distal nephron (III → I → V → VI → II → IV).
